tier_justification: Textbook facts about yes/no analyzers (always-false is trivially sound) and elementary order facts (subsets of the good programs form a down-set closed under union), restated for Boolean checkers.
plain_claim: For a fixed semantic predicate good, a checker is sound iff it is pointwise below the classical oracle of good (the possibly noncomputable Boolean function that is true exactly on good programs); hence the set of sound checkers contains rejectAll, is downward closed in the pointwise order, and is closed under the pointwise or of two checkers that are sound for the same good.

hypotheses.name: hle : CheckerLE c₁ c₂ (sound_of_checkerLE_of_sound)
hypotheses.purpose: c1 must not accept anything c2 rejects; otherwise c1 can accept programs about which c2's soundness says nothing.

hypotheses.name: h₂ : Sound good c₂ (sound_of_checkerLE_of_sound)
hypotheses.purpose: Soundness has to come from somewhere; the order only transfers it downward.

hypotheses.name: h₁ : Sound good c₁ (sound_orChecker_of_sound_of_sound)
hypotheses.purpose: Accepting on c1's say-so requires c1 to be sound.

hypotheses.name: h₂ : Sound good c₂ (sound_orChecker_of_sound_of_sound)
hypotheses.purpose: Symmetric to h1.

nonvacuity_witness: Both sides of the characterization occur: evenExact is below the oracle of evenGood and acceptAll is not (so soundness is not trivial in the toy instance). The closure hypotheses hold for evenBelowTen <= evenExact with evenExact sound, and for the two sound single-program checkers (· == 0) and (· == 2).
non_claims: The oracle is a mathematical function, in general not computable; nothing says an implementable tool attains the top of this down-set. For decidable good the oracle equals fun p => decide (good p) (classicalOracle_eq_decide); nothing more is claimed about decidability.
Uses classical logic (Classical.choice via the oracle's definition).
Does not say soundness is upward closed (it is not: rejectAll <= acceptAll), nor that a more conservative checker is preferable; conservativeness costs completeness, which is not measured here.
Only binary (hence finite) disjunctions are covered; arbitrary unions of sound checkers are not stated (in the classical model they are also sound, but that is not a theorem of this package).

Closure under or needs both checkers to be sound for the same predicate good. Combining real tools that assume different language dialects, memory models or undefined-behavior conventions and accepting when either accepts is sound only for the disjunction of their predicates, not for either stricter one.

Polarity: Sound models tools whose true answer certifies goodness. For bug finders that promise no false alarms (every reported problem is real), the guarantee is the dual one, c p = false implies not good p; the order is reversed and the degenerate tool is acceptAll (report nothing), not rejectAll. Nothing here is stated for that polarity.
Says nothing about completeness, running time, or termination of any tool.
prior_art: X. Rival and K. Yi, Introduction to Static Analysis: An Abstract Interpretation Perspective, MIT Press, 2020, Chapter 1. Defines soundness (answer true implies the property) and completeness (the property implies answer true) of a yes/no analysis as here (Sound; CompleteOn with F = all programs), and notes that the analysis answering false everywhere is trivially sound and the one answering true everywhere trivially complete.

P. Cousot and R. Cousot, 'Abstract interpretation: a unified lattice model for static analysis of programs by construction or approximation of fixpoints', POPL 1977, pp. 238-252, doi:10.1145/512950.512973. Source of the soundness-as-over-approximation framing of static analysis. Correspondence (our reading, not a statement of the paper): sound abstractions over-approximate the reachable behaviors and form an up-set whose top element carries no information; a yes/no checker derived from an abstraction accepts p only if the over-approximation lies within the safe behaviors. That passage reverses the order, so the up-set of sound over-approximations corresponds to the down-set of sound checkers, and the top element to rejectAll at the bottom.

P. W. O'Hearn, 'Incorrectness logic', Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(POPL):1-32, 2020, doi:10.1145/3371078. Under-approximate reasoning for bug finding: reported bugs are guaranteed to be real (no false positives), at the price of missed bugs. Cited for the opposite polarity: for such tools the degenerate tool reports nothing, which corresponds to acceptAll rather than rejectAll; this package states results for the certifying polarity only.
design_question: Can a framework exclude degenerate tools (reject-all) using soundness-style laws alone, or does it need an additional positive requirement?

tier_justification: Immediate consequence of the textbook fact that rejecting everything is sound (R1a), stated as a fact about laws.
plain_claim: Any law L satisfied by every sound checker is also satisfied by rejectAll; consequently no law implied by soundness alone can exclude rejectAll.

hypotheses.name: hL : ∀ c, Sound good c → L c
hypotheses.purpose: The law is implied by soundness (every sound checker satisfies it).

nonvacuity_witness: L := Sound evenGood satisfies hL.
non_claims: Does not say no law can exclude rejectAll: laws not implied by soundness (anchors, completeness on a fragment, checked two-sided answers) can (positive control; R2a, R6e, R4f).
Does not say that excluding rejectAll requires excluding an honest tool: the law fun c => c ≠ rejectAll excludes rejectAll and no other checker.
Stated for the certifying polarity; for bug finders that promise no false alarms the degenerate tool is acceptAll (see R1a).
Says nothing about intensional evidence (source inspection) or about laws on richer outputs such as certificates (R4).

tier_justification: Restatement of version-space facts for an unrestricted hypothesis space: the empty hypothesis is consistent iff there are no positive examples, and the disjunction of the positive examples is consistent when they are all good.
plain_claim: The anchored law (sound and accepts every anchor in the finite list A) excludes rejectAll iff A is nonempty, for every good and every A whether or not the anchors are good; and if every anchor is good, the anchored law admits the allowlist checker that accepts exactly the members of A.

hypotheses.name: [DecidableEq P] (allowlist_anchoredSound_of_anchors_good)
hypotheses.purpose: Needed only to define the allowlist as a Boolean function; the allowlist does not depend on which instance is used, and one always exists classically.

hypotheses.name: hA : ∀ a ∈ A, good a (allowlist_anchoredSound_of_anchors_good)
hypotheses.purpose: Accepting a bad anchor contradicts soundness, so with a bad anchor nothing is admitted.

nonvacuity_witness: Both sides of the first statement occur (anchors [0] exclude rejectAll; no anchors admit it); the anchors [0, 2] are good for evenGood.
non_claims: If some anchor is bad, the law excludes every checker, so 'excludes rejectAll' is then vacuous; that the law admits anything needs good anchors (second statement).
Excluding rejectAll does not exclude near-trivial tools: the allowlist of the anchors is admitted (second statement; R2c).
Does not say the allowlist is the only admitted checker, nor that an allowlist is an acceptable tool for a framework; it says the anchored law cannot tell it apart from honest tools.
prior_art: T. M. Mitchell, 'Generalization as search', Artificial Intelligence 18(2):203-226, 1982, doi:10.1016/0004-3702(82)90040-6. Version spaces: the hypotheses consistent with labeled examples, ordered by generality and represented by their most specific and most general boundary sets.

T. M. Mitchell, Machine Learning, McGraw-Hill, 1997, Chapter 2 (concept learning, the version space representation theorem, and the unbiased learner whose hypothesis space contains every subset of the instances). For that learner the most specific consistent hypothesis is the disjunction of the positive examples and no instance outside the training examples is classified unanimously. Correspondence (our reading): checkers are hypotheses, the pointwise order is the generality order, anchors and suite entries are labeled examples, and soundness acts as a negative example at every bad program (infinitely many in general, unlike a finite training set); the results cited here restate that picture in this vocabulary.
design_question: What do positive anchors and finite conformance suites actually force on an admitted tool, and can they exclude lookup-table tools?

tier_justification: Restatement of the unanimous-vote facts for an unbiased version space (only training examples are classified unanimously), with soundness playing the role of a negative example at every bad program.
plain_claim: If every anchor in A is good, a program is accepted by every checker that the anchored law admits iff it is an anchor, and is rejected by every admitted checker iff it is bad; explicitly, for any good program p not in A, the allowlists of A and of p :: A are both admitted and disagree on p.

hypotheses.name: hA : ∀ a ∈ A, good a (forced_accept_iff_mem_anchors_of_anchors_good)
hypotheses.purpose: With a bad anchor the law admits nothing and every program is vacuously forced to be accepted.

hypotheses.name: hA : ∀ a ∈ A, good a (forced_reject_iff_not_good_of_anchors_good)
hypotheses.purpose: With a bad anchor the law admits nothing and every program is vacuously forced to be rejected.

hypotheses.name: [DecidableEq P] (anchoredSound_admits_allowlists_disagreeing_at_good_nonanchor_of_anchors_good)
hypotheses.purpose: Needed only to define allowlists; they do not depend on the instance.

hypotheses.name: hA : ∀ a ∈ A, good a (witness family)
hypotheses.purpose: Otherwise neither allowlist is admitted.

hypotheses.name: hp : good p (witness family)
hypotheses.purpose: Otherwise the allowlist of p :: A is unsound.

hypotheses.name: hpA : p ∉ A (witness family)
hypotheses.purpose: Otherwise the allowlist of A accepts p, so the two allowlists do not disagree on p.

nonvacuity_witness: Anchors [0, 2] are good for evenGood; for the witness family, anchors [0] and the good non-anchor 2.
non_claims: Concerns acceptance forced by the anchored law alone. Laws with further requirements can force more: completeness on a fragment (R6f), or a relational requirement linking answers on different programs, such as 'accepting p forces accepting 2 * p', which with the single anchor 2 forces infinitely many acceptances and excludes every allowlist while admitting a conservative, incomplete checker (doubling_law_admits_fourOrTwo_excludes_every_allowlist).
The anchored law is a pointwise law on finitely many inputs; nothing here is claimed for relational or metamorphic laws beyond the single example cited above.
Does not say an admitted checker can be found algorithmically; the witness for a good p is the allowlist of p :: A, which presupposes knowing that p is good.

The first two statements have no DecidableEq P hypothesis; their proofs build the witness allowlists with classical decidable equality (Classical.choice), and the forced-acceptance statement, quantified over all types, implies double-negation elimination, so it is not constructive. With a DecidableEq P instance the witnesses are the computable allowlists of the third statement.
Exhibits two admitted checkers for each good non-anchor; does not enumerate all admitted checkers, and does not quantify how many anchors are needed for any practical purpose.

tier_justification: Restatement of the fact that the most specific hypothesis consistent with labeled examples in an unrestricted hypothesis space is the disjunction of the positive examples, read as the informal lookup-table argument against finite behavioral tests.
plain_claim: For a finite test suite T (programs with expected answers): if some checker c passes T, then the lookup table of T (accept exactly the programs that T expects to be accepted) passes T and is pointwise below c, so it is the least checker passing T; if moreover c is sound, the lookup table is sound. So no law of the form 'sound and passes T' admits some checker while excluding the lookup table of T.

hypotheses.name: [DecidableEq P]
hypotheses.purpose: Needed only to define the lookup table; it does not depend on the instance.

hypotheses.name: hc : Sound good c (tableChecker_sound_passes_le_of_sound_passes)
hypotheses.purpose: Soundness of the table is inherited from c via the order; a suite passed only by unsound checkers can expect acceptance of a bad program.

hypotheses.name: hT : Passes c T (tableChecker_sound_passes_le_of_sound_passes)
hypotheses.purpose: Some sound checker must pass T, so T expects acceptance only of good programs.

hypotheses.name: hT : Passes c T (tableChecker_passes_and_le_of_passes)
hypotheses.purpose: Without a passing checker the table need not be below c (consistent suite, c = rejectAll) and need not pass T (inconsistent suite).

nonvacuity_witness: evenExact is sound for evenGood and passes [(0, true), (1, false), (2, true)].
non_claims: The table is built from T: the theorem is about a suite fixed before the table is chosen. It does not say a single table passes every suite, nor that a table fixed in advance passes suites chosen afterwards (held-out or randomized tests are not modeled).

Does not say tests are useless. Nearby laws exclude lookup tables while admitting honest tools: completeness on an infinite fragment (first positive control; R6g), and, without any completeness requirement, the relational law 'passes [(2, true)] and accepting p forces accepting 2 * p', which admits the conservative, incomplete checker fourOrTwo and excludes the lookup table of every finite suite (second positive control).
The impossibility concerns only laws of the form 'sound and passes T', which are pointwise laws on finitely many inputs.

Says nothing about intensional checks (code inspection) that could detect a table. Conclusions about untested inputs from finite testing need hypotheses on the implementation under test (as in the testing literature cited); none is assumed here.

Formal account of when passing a finite test set establishes correctness: only under conditions on the test selection criterion (reliability and validity) that tie the tested inputs to the untested ones.

M.-C. Gaudel, 'Testing can be formal, too', TAPSOFT '95, LNCS 915, pp. 82-96, 1995, doi:10.1007/3-540-59293-8_188. Specification-based testing in which a finite test set is justified only together with explicit hypotheses on the implementation under test (uniformity, regularity). The lookup-table statement here is the situation without any such hypothesis.

N. Block, 'Psychologism and Behaviorism', The Philosophical Review 90(1):5-43, 1981, doi:10.2307/2184371. The lookup-table thought experiment: a system that reproduces any finite stretch of required behavior by table lookup, used to argue that behavioral tests alone cannot certify how behavior is produced. Philosophical background only; no formal statement there corresponds to these theorems.

tier_justification: Restatement of the definition of an extensional property and of function extensionality, for laws on tool implementations, with a concrete instance.
plain_claim: If a law on tool implementations is extensional (respects pointwise equality of behavior) and two implementations have the same behavior on every program, the law holds of one iff it holds of the other; every law stated directly on Boolean checkers is extensional (by function extensionality), so for laws on input-output behavior the hypothesis is automatic; in particular, in the toy model no extensional law separates the specific arithmetic implementation honestImpl ('accept p iff p < 10 and p is even') from the specific lookup table tableImpl ([0, 2, 4, 6, 8]).

hypotheses.name: hL : ExtensionalLaw run L (extensionalLaw_iff_of_same_behavior)
hypotheses.purpose: The law must look only at behavior; an intensional law can separate behaviorally identical implementations.

hypotheses.name: hij : ∀ p, run i p = run j p (extensionalLaw_iff_of_same_behavior)
hypotheses.purpose: The two implementations must agree everywhere; an extensional law can separate implementations that differ on one program.

hypotheses.name: hL : ExtensionalLaw toyRun L (extensionalLaw_cannot_separate_honestImpl_from_tableImpl)
hypotheses.purpose: Only behavior-respecting laws are blind to the difference; IsStructural is not extensional and separates the two implementations.

nonvacuity_witness: The law 'behavior is sound for evenGood' is extensional and honestImpl, tableImpl have the same behavior; soundness for evenGood, as a law on Boolean checkers, instantiates the second statement.
non_claims: Definitional: the first statement is the definition of extensionality read in both directions, the second is function extensionality (a theorem in Lean, derived from Quot.sound; in a setting without it the statement would have to be assumed), the third instantiates the first. The value is in naming the barrier, not in depth.

Intensional laws, i.e. predicates on the implementation itself (source inspection, build provenance; here IsStructural), are outside the barrier and can separate such implementations (positive control). Requiring richer output, such as a certificate with each answer, is not intensional: the barrier applies again to the richer behavior, and a lookup table that stores precomputed valid certificates has the same certified output as an honest tool on the same finite set (cachedCertTool_eq_boundedHonestTool; R4e).

The toy instance concerns two implementations that accept the same finite set. An honest checker that accepts infinitely many programs has no finite table with the same behavior, and extensional laws can separate it from every finite table (R6g; the positive controls of R2f).

Not Rice's theorem, and a different notion of extensionality: ExtensionalLaw is extensionality at the level of tools (two implementations give the same answer on every program), not semantic extensionality of target programs (a property of programs that depends only on the function a program computes). A law on tools may distinguish two semantically equivalent programs. Nothing about decidability is stated or used.
Does not say behavioral laws are useless; they constrain behavior, just not implementation.
prior_art: H. G. Rice, 'Classes of recursively enumerable sets and their decision problems', Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 74(2):358-366, 1953, doi:10.1090/S0002-9947-1953-0053041-6. Rice's theorem: a class of recursively enumerable sets has a decidable index set only if it is trivial. Context only, and a different notion of extensionality: Rice's hypothesis concerns properties of programs that depend only on the function a program computes, whereas ExtensionalLaw concerns laws on tools that depend only on the tools' answers. Not formalized here.

R. Bruni, R. Giacobazzi, R. Gori, I. Garcia-Contreras and D. Illustrates the difference between tool-level extensionality (here) and semantic extensionality of target programs.

Philosophical background only; no formal statement there corresponds to these theorems.

tier_justification: Core soundness argument of proof-carrying code, certifying algorithms and verified validators, re-derived in the toy model.
plain_claim: If a fixed verifier V is sound (V p w = true implies good p), then for every one-sided certifying tool t the induced checker (accept p iff t p = some w and V p w = true; silence or a rejected certificate means reject) is sound, whatever t does.

hypotheses.name: hV : VerifierSound good V
hypotheses.purpose: The trust is carried by V; with an unsound V some tool yields an unsound checker.

nonvacuity_witness: halfV (w certifies p iff w + w = p) is sound for evenGood; the lying tool that always outputs 7 is an admissible t and its induced checker accepts 14.
non_claims: Does not transfer completeness (R4c, R4d). With two-sided certification and a requirement of checked answers on a fragment, completeness on that fragment is forced (R4f).
Assumes the framework, not the tool, runs V on each output; a tool that reports 'accepted' without its certificate being checked is outside the model.

certChecker V t passes the original program p itself to V. In an implementation, if the untrusted tool can alter the program, or supply a certificate for a transformed representation that V does not relate back to p, soundness can fail; any parser or verification-condition generator that maps p to proof obligations belongs to V and hence to the trusted base.

Rules out unsound tools without inspecting their internals, but does not rule out lookup tables: a table that stores precomputed valid certificates for finitely many programs induces a sound checker and has the same output as an honest tool on the same finite set (cachedCertTool_eq_boundedHonestTool).
Says nothing about the cost of checking or of finding certificates.
prior_art: G. C. Necula, 'Proof-carrying code', POPL 1997, pp. 106-119, doi:10.1145/263699.263712. Untrusted code is shipped with a safety proof that the code consumer validates with a small proof checker against a fixed safety policy (one-sided: code without a valid proof is simply refused).

R. M. McConnell, K. Mehlhorn, S. Näher and P. Schweitzer, 'Certifying algorithms', Computer Science Review 5(2):119-161, 2011, doi:10.1016/j.cosrev.2010.09.009. Algorithms that output a witness with each answer, checked by a simple checker, so that trust moves from the algorithm to the checker. For decision problems a certifying algorithm supplies a witness for either answer (for bipartiteness: a 2-coloring for yes, an odd cycle for no); that is the two-sided shape of R4f, not the one-sided certChecker of R4a-R4e, in which a rejection needs no witness.

J.-B. Tristan and X. Leroy, 'Formal verification of translation validators: a case study on instruction scheduling optimizations', POPL 2008, pp. 17-27, doi:10.1145/1328438.1328444. A translation validator verified in Coq checks each run of an untrusted optimization; soundness of the validator gives correctness of every validated run, whatever the untrusted transformation does. A mechanized instance of the R4a pattern.

E. Alkassar, S. Böhme, K. Mehlhorn and C. Rizkallah, 'A framework for the verification of certifying computations', Journal of Automated Reasoning 52(3):241-273, 2014, doi:10.1007/s10817-013-9289-2 (conference version CAV 2011, LNCS 6806, pp. 67-82, doi:10.1007/978-3-642-22110-1_7). Verifies witness checkers (with VCC) and the mathematical witness properties (with Isabelle/HOL), so that certified computations can be trusted without trusting the algorithm.

R. Thiemann and C. Sternagel, 'Certification of termination proofs using CeTA', TPHOLs 2009, LNCS 5674, pp. 452-468, doi:10.1007/978-3-642-03359-9_31. A certifier, generated from an Isabelle/HOL formalization, that checks termination proofs produced by untrusted tools; a mechanized trusted verifier for certificates.

A. Pnueli, M. Siegel and E. Singerman, 'Translation validation', TACAS 1998, LNCS 1384, pp. 151-166, doi:10.1007/BFb0054170. Instead of verifying a compiler once, each individual run is followed by a validation that the produced target implements the source.

M. Blum and S. Kannan, 'Designing programs that check their work', Journal of the ACM 42(1):269-291, 1995, doi:10.1145/200836.200880. tier_justification: Exact unfolding of completeness for the one-sided certifying pipeline, with its consequence for the verifier.
plain_claim: The checker induced by a one-sided tool t and verifier V is complete on fragment F iff for every good program p in F the tool outputs some certificate w with V p w = true; in particular, completeness on F requires V to accept some certificate for every good program of F.

hypotheses.name: h : CompleteOn good F (certChecker V t) (verifierCompleteOn_of_certChecker_completeOn)
hypotheses.purpose: Without a complete pipeline nothing forces V to have certificates (e.g. rejectAllV has none).

nonvacuity_witness: Both sides of the equivalence occur for halfV on all programs (the honest tool satisfies the right-hand side, the silent tool does not); the honest tool's pipeline is complete on all programs.
non_claims: Completeness is a property of neither the tool alone nor the verifier alone: it needs certificates to exist in V's language for every good program of F (second statement; with rejectAllV no tool succeeds, no_tool_completeOn_rejectAllV) and the tool to find them; verifier completeness alone does not suffice (R4d).

Concerns one-sided certification, in which a rejection needs no evidence. Under two-sided certification with checked answers required on F, a tool that rejects a good program of F is excluded instead (R4f).

hypotheses.purpose: The answer at p must actually be forced; an invariant law that forces nothing transfers nothing.

plain_claim: A checker is sound and complete on F iff the same checker is sound everywhere and decides good on F; hence, for any class K of admissible checkers, the law has a satisfier in K iff some checker in K is sound and decides good on F. The closure statement's non-vacuity witness with K = all checkers is degenerate in one respect: that class already contains a sound decider, so the soundness repair (restricting an unsound decider of good on F to F with the decider of F) is not needed there. Background from outside this package, not a result of it: if P were program texts of a Turing-complete language, K the computable checkers, and good a nontrivial property of the partial function a program computes, Rice's theorem (H. G. Rice 1953, listed under prior art) would make the full-fragment right-hand side false, so the law on all programs would have no computable satisfier. None of this is formalized or proved here: the package defines neither program texts nor computability, and it neither proves nor refutes the general claim that every property and fragment admit an implementable (computable) checker that is sound and complete on that fragment. The remark also leaves the standard alternatives open: properties that are not semantic (e.g. syntactic or type-structural ones) may be decidable; restricting completeness to a fragment F that is decided in K reduces the question to deciding good on F (closure statement); and procedures that may diverge are outside this model of total checkers P -> Bool.

Completeness on an infinite fragment is one way to exclude every finite table, not the only one: a relational law with a single anchor ('accepting p forces accepting 2 * p') also excludes every allowlist while admitting a conservative, incomplete checker (doubling_law_admits_fourOrTwo_excludes_every_allowlist).
prior_art: N. Block, 'Psychologism and Behaviorism', The Philosophical Review 90(1):5-43, 1981, doi:10.2307/2184371. The lookup-table thought experiment: a system that reproduces any finite stretch of required behavior by table lookup, used to argue that behavioral tests alone cannot certify how behavior is produced. Philosophical background only; no formal statement there corresponds to these theorems.
design_question: When a framework requires soundness plus completeness on a fragment, when is the law satisfiable, when does it lock out the do-nothing tool or all lookup tables, and what does 'decidable' mean in the model?

tier_justification: Counterexample to a tempting simplification of R6c ('satisfiable in K iff good restricted to F is K-decidable').
plain_claim: 'good restricted to F is decided by some checker in K' does not imply that the law 'sound and complete on F' has a satisfier in K: with K = {acceptAll} and good = F = (p = 0), acceptAll decides good on F but is unsound off F.
nonvacuity_witness: It is itself a concrete instance.
non_claims: The class used does not contain a decider for F. For classes closed under pointwise and that do contain one, the simplification holds (R6c, closure statement; this counterexample is its tightness witness for that hypothesis, cex_decides_on_iff_needs_decidedIn).
